newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka eases ban on medicine to rebel area.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka eases ban on medicine to rebel area.

text.p: The Sri Lankan army on Tuesday eased a ban on medicine to parts of the northern Wanni region held by Tamil Tiger rebels, government officials said.

They said the move, announced by the army's population and resource control division at northcentral Vavuniya, gateway to the Wanni, followed reports that a shortage of medicine had caused the spread of disease.

People going to the Wanni, most of which is under the control of Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), can now take small amounts of medicine such as anti-malarial drugs and vitamins, officials said.
It was not immediately clear if pain killers and antibiotics will now be allowed.
Restrictions on movement of medicine were imposed early last year when security forces were on the offensive against the LTTE in the northern Jaffna peninsula.
The rebels, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of the Indian Ocean island, are known to confiscate government supplies of food and drugs.
Government officials said malaria was spreading among residents and refugees in the Wanni because of the shortage of drugs.
Some 200,000 refugees are in the Wanni after fleeing their homes to avoid fighting between the army and the rebels.
The army is now hunting the Tigers in their eastern jungle lairs but the rebels have mostly avoided a battle.
Rebel radio intercepted by the army indicated a LTTE area leader named Srikanth died in an airstrike on a guerrilla base in eastern Batticaloa district on Sunday, military officials said.

State radio said up to 30 rebels were believed killed in the pre-emptive strike on the camp after intelligence reports that the Tigers were concentrating in the area to launch attacks on military bases.
At least five soldiers were killed and four wounded when their tractor was blown up by a rebel landmine in Kallar, in northeastern Trincomalee, a military statement said.
The Tigers were not immediately available for comment on the military's reports of the latest action.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war. The rebels say the toll is much higher.
